sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
sections.body_md:
Newton's method looks for a root by replacing the map with its tangent and solving the tangent exactly. In one variable the picture is a graph and a tangent line. The line meets the axis at one point, provided the slope is not zero, and that meeting point is the next guess. The tangent is then redrawn at the new guess. Each iteration throws away the old line.

The algebra is the same in several variables. The Jacobian times the step equals the negative of the map, and the point moves by the step. If the Jacobian is square and invertible, this is also the Gauss-Newton step on the sum of squares of the components, because the Gram matrix can be canceled. If the Jacobian is singular, the tangent does not determine one step. A zero derivative in one variable is the horizontal-tangent case: the line never meets the axis, or it lies on the axis.

The starting point chooses which root is approached, and it can choose a root that is not the nearest. A cubic with three real roots has a start between two of them whose tangent lands on the third. An affine map with a nonzero slope finishes in one step from every start, because the tangent is the map. A tiny slope makes the correction large, so the next guess can leave the neighborhood where the tangent was fair.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The scalar update and the vector step are
\[
t^+ = t - \frac{g(t)}{g'(t)}, \qquad J_F(x)\, d = -F(x).
\]
A zero derivative, or a singular Jacobian, leaves the step undefined.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(g(t) = t^2 - 6\) at \(t = 5\). The value is \(19\) and the derivative is \(10\). The correction is \(19/10\), and the next guess subtracts it from \(5\).

The pier guess is 3.1. The root of this parabola is not \(3.1\). The tangent was drawn at \(5\), where the slope is already steep, and one hit only gets part of the way. Starting on the other side of the axis would follow a negative slope toward the negative root. A start at a point where the derivative vanishes would have no step at all.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Using the derivative of \(t^2\) as \(2\), rather than as \(2t\), divides by the wrong slope and lands at the wrong point. A second slip is to treat a zero derivative as a root. The function value has to vanish as well. A third is to expect the nearest root. The tangent, not the distance to the roots, chooses the next point. A fourth is to reuse the old derivative at the new point. The method rebuilds the tangent because the slope of a curved map has changed.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The same tangent step applied to the gradient equation is Newton's method for minimization. The Jacobian of the gradient is the Hessian, so the step can be attracted to a maximum or a saddle when that Hessian is not positive definite. Farther on, a primal-dual interior-point iteration uses this root step on a perturbed system of complementarity conditions, rebuilding the tangent at every new primal and dual point.
